article.articleHeadline: An urban malaria-carrying mosquito that is insecticide-resistant is spreading across Africa.
article.articleSummary: An urban malaria-carrying mosquito Anopheles stephensi, originally from Asia, is expanding across Africa and showing resistance to all known insecticides. It tolerates dry seasons and thrives in urban waters, contrasting with traditional rural vectors, raising malaria risk in megacities such as Lagos (Nigeria) and Kinshasa (DR Congo), each with about 20 million residents lacking prior malaria immunity. The spread has accelerated since first arriving in the Horn of Africa over a decade ago; genomic analyses confirm multi-country insecticide resistance, complicating control. In Djibouti, cases rose from 27 in 2012 to about 70,000 annually; Ethiopia reports a similar pattern. Globally, malaria causes about 600,000 deaths per year. The mosquito’s urban adaptability could transform transmission dynamics, demanding new interventions; climate warming could broaden distribution to Europe, though local surveillance mitigates large outbreaks, with isolated autochthonous dengue cases noted in France linked to urban vectors.

article.articleHeadline: From Hantavirus to Ebola: Rebuilding Trust in Health and Biosecurity Governance
article.articleSummary: April 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak aboard MV Hondius: 13 cases and 3 deaths; more than 600 contacts across 32 countries and territories. Epidemiology and genomic data indicate a point-source event with limited secondary transmission, with the source under investigation and possible pre-embarkation exposures tied to travel, ecologies, and rodent habitats. Bundibugyo Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda have escalated to a regional emergency; no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists, so surveillance, clinical preparedness, community engagement, and cross-border coordination are essential. Governance challenges include transparent, timely risk communication and erosion of trust, illustrated by WHO briefings on May 7, 2026 and US trust in scientists at 36% in April 2025. The piece advocates a Planetary Health approach and ASEAN One Health coordination, integrating ACPHEED with environmental indicators, mobility data, and surveillance for early detection in Southeast Asia.

It also notes discussions about the hopeful role of new vaccines and increased international support. Mpox in Madagascar: through the first seven months of 2026, 4,798 notified cases (3,146 laboratory-confirmed) and 22 deaths since mid-December 2025; vaccination prioritized for close contacts, frontline health workers, and high-risk groups, including sex workers in dense urban and port areas; Clade 1b identified in sequences. article.articleHeadline: SADC battles cash crunch as DRC conflict, Ebola test region's resilience

Chairperson Ambassador Tebogo Seokolo warned of a complex regional landscape marked by geopolitical instability, economic volatility, climate shocks, and security threats, with ongoing instability in eastern DRC and a recent Ebola outbreak testing regional resilience. He stressed peace and security as top preoccupations. He urged accelerated industrialisation and greater investment in infrastructure, trade, food and nutrition security, energy, climate resilience, healthcare, gender equality and youth empowerment. Finance remains under serious pressure as donor funding declines. Delegates will review implementation of prior decisions, sustainable financing, reforms, and measures to boost SADC effectiveness.

article.articleHeadline: QDENGA approval hailed by doctors amid seasonal dengue spike in Karnataka
article.articleSummary: India’s first dengue vaccine, QDENGA by Takeda, has been approved by the Drugs Controller General of India for individuals aged 4–60 years and is designed to protect against all four dengue serotypes without prior dengue screening. In Karnataka’s monsoon-driven dengue spike, doctors welcome the approval but note it is unlikely to be available during the current season in Karnataka. Clinical data show about an 80% reduction in symptomatic dengue and roughly a 90% reduction in hospitalisations during the first year after vaccination; protection against hospitalisation remains high at about 85% for up to four-and-a-half to five years. Dengue can be caused by four serotypes; many infections are asymptomatic, but severe dengue can cause bleeding, fluid buildup, internal haemorrhage, and death, making vaccination a significant preventive step in states like Karnataka.

article.articleHeadline: What are the symptoms of cholera, the disease that still poses a risk to millions of people?
article.articleSummary: Cholera, a persistent global threat, originated in India with a 1817 pandemic and reached Veracruz, Mexico, in 1833. The article notes one of the worst outbreaks occurred in Iztapalapa, Mexico City. Today, cholera remains a public health risk in regions with limited potable water and sanitation. The CDC estimates 1.3–4 million cases and 21,000–143,000 deaths annually worldwide. Symptoms include acute watery diarrhea, vomiting, and muscle cramps, which can rapidly cause severe dehydration without treatment. Immediate rehydration with electrolyte-rich fluids is the cornerstone of therapy, with antibiotics reserved for specific cases. In Mexico, Vida Suero Oral has long been used since the 1980s to prevent diarrheal complications and dehydration. Prevention hinges on drinking safe water, good hand hygiene, proper food washing and disinfection, and avoiding contaminated products. Imported/exported cases are not detailed in this article.

article.articleHeadline: CG: A disease that has suddenly spread in your village or neighborhood, do not panic; report it directly on the IHIP portal as soon as two patients with the same disease are observed.
article.articleSummary: As of August 6, 2026, in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, two or more cases of the same disease in a village, neighborhood, or settlement should be reported on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) to flag a potential outbreak. The IHIP, part of India's IDSP, enables Community Based Surveillance by allowing any citizen to log suspicious health events online. Reports trigger rapid investigation, sample collection, treatment, and containment measures to prevent escalation. When submitting, provide name, mobile number, age, gender, address, occupation, date, place, and a brief description of the illness; photos or documents can be uploaded as evidence. Her trek underscores how frontline workers in Manipur's remote hills must reach villages with limited road access to sustain immunisation and maintain the cold chain. As of 2026-08-06, IPPI continues to be a critical measure to keep polio at bay.

Health authorities are distributing doxycycline as chemoprophylaxis: adults are advised a 200 mg dose once weekly after meals, to be swallowed with plenty of water, and to remain upright for at least 30 minutes after intake. The preventive course should continue weekly for as long as contact with floodwater persists. Pregnant women, lactating mothers, and children under eight should not take doxycycline. Treatment should follow a physician’s instructions; if fever, body aches, or eye redness occur, individuals should not self-treat but seek care immediately. The health department is coordinating distribution in camps.

article.articleHeadline: Rising risk of these dangerous diseases in dairy cattle during the rainy season; adopt these essential measures.
article.articleSummary: As monsoon arrives, dairy cattle face elevated risks of viral and bacterial infections and parasitic diseases, threatening milk yield. Diseases highlighted include galghonto, adharangi, Black Quarter (Blackleg), and Foot-and-Mouth Disease, plus Fascioliasis (liver fluke) from contaminated water and fodder. External parasites such as ticks, lice, and fleas drive Babesiosis and Theileriosis, with fever and red urine possible; snail-like vectors spread parasites. To reduce risk, maintain proper housing: Head-to-Head systems allow easier feeding but raise cross-infection risk; Tail-to-Tail systems reduce contact and aid ventilation and cleaning. Rural farms favor Head-to-Head for space and feed management; urban dairies prefer Tail-to-Tail for hygiene and housing density. Mastitis risk increases during calving; keep barns clean, dry, ventilated, and elevate resting areas to avoid mud. Provide balanced diets, avoid moldy fodder, ensure clean water, and perform deworming and vaccination against mastitis-linked pathogens and Foot-and-Mouth disease during the monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: How early screening can beat 'silent killers' Hepatitis B and C
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-06, Hepatitis B and C often progress silently for years, risking cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer before warning signs appear. In India, about 300 million people live with HBV or HCV unaware of infection. Early screening via a simple blood test is the key to prevention: HBV can be controlled with antivirals and vaccinated against, while most Hepatitis C infections are now curable with oral medicines taken for a few months. Transmission varies: HBV through infected blood, unprotected sex, or mother-to-child; HCV mainly through infected blood via unsafe injections, unsterile medical or dental procedures, tattooing, or sharing needles. High-risk groups include family history, healthcare workers, pre-screened blood transfusion recipients, dialysis patients, multiple sexual partners, injection drug users, and persistently abnormal liver tests. Do not wait for symptoms; early diagnosis reduces risk of cirrhosis and cancer.

article.articleHeadline: IIT-G develops low-cost device to detect toxic metals, bacteria in water
article.articleSummary: IIT Guwahati unveils E-Eye, a portable optical sensor that detects toxic metals (arsenic, lead, iron, chromium), fluoride, and Escherichia coli in water. Priced about Rs 3,500 with per-test cost around Rs 2, the device enables on-site water-quality checks at water sources, including rural areas lacking laboratories. It uses a colorimetric reaction whose intensity corresponds to contaminant concentration, read via optical sensing, converted to digital data, and transmitted wirelessly to water-treatment facilities. E-Eye’s results have shown comparability with standard UV-Visible and Atomic Absorption spectrometry across more than 2,700 samples. Operates on Beer-Lambert law, combining optics with digital electronics. Supports Jal Jeevan Mission goals for safe rural tap water; applicable to environmental/biological samples and foods. Commercialization via ENVIONIX Labs Pvt Ltd, with plans for solar panels and cloud connectivity; collaborators include KIIT Bhubaneswar and Ramakrishna Mission Residential College, Kolkata.

article.articleHeadline: Experts call for advanced diagnostics, AI and stronger UDST to accelerate India's TB elimination drive
article.articleSummary: Two-day National Conclave and Policy Dialogue on Tuberculosis in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, urged strengthening Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing (UDST) and adopting advanced diagnostics—molecular tests, genotypic testing, targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS)—and artificial intelligence to accelerate India’s TB elimination. Experts stressed early detection of drug-resistant TB, streamlined patient care pathways, digital systems and real-time monitoring as essential. Inaugurated by Dr. Digambar Behera, the forum highlighted India’s status as possessing the world’s highest TB burden, with challenges in selecting effective regimens and ensuring diagnostic accuracy before treatment. The gathering focused on field-level challenges in remote, tribal and hard-to-reach areas, calling for actionable measures to improve sample collection, transport, reporting, treatment initiation and follow-up. Official data show a 21% decline in TB cases and 28% in TB deaths from 2015–2024; the TB-Mukt Bharat drive has screened over 200 million people since Dec 7, 2024, and AI-enabled programs have aided diagnosis of over 2.8 million TB patients nationwide.

article.articleHeadline: Meningococcal outbreak: Doc says do not panic, be vigilant
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-06, a localized meningococcal outbreak in Peren district, Nagaland, involves 7 pediatric cases admitted to CIHSR; one suspected death awaiting laboratory confirmation; six other cases discharged. All cases are from Peren district. Neisseria meningitidis is the causative agent, with serotype A being most common in India. Transmission occurs person-to-person via respiratory droplets and saliva, amplified by crowding; sneezing or coughing without masks and sharing utensils or cigarettes facilitate spread. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, and stiff neck; in advanced stages, red petechial rashes or purpura with thrombocytopenia, leading to bleeding, hypotension, and shock may occur. Third-generation antibiotics can effectively treat the infection. Prevention emphasizes vaccination (9 months to 55 years), use of masks, good hygiene, and rapid medical consultation; close contacts may receive prophylaxis. Public messaging stresses vigilance, not panic.

article.articleHeadline: Closing the gaps in the fight against hepatitis
article.articleSummary: Hepatitis B and C screening expansion shows early progress under the StITCH project in the Philippines, where more than 24,000 people were screened for hepatitis B and many linked to care and started on treatment; in Vietnam, over 85,000 were screened for hepatitis B and about 69,000 for hepatitis C. article.articleHeadline: Where do E. coli bacteria commonly occur, and what diseases can they cause?

A Vietnamese case from Ninh Bình involves a 72-year-old man who developed E. coli meningitis; initial symptoms were headache and altered consciousness, with cerebrospinal fluid confirming E. coli meningitis. Expanded testing revealed concurrent Angiostrongylus cantonensis (roundworm) infection; the worm does not directly cause meningitis but larvae can enable bacteria to enter the bloodstream, leading to bacteremia and meningitis. Treatment included antibiotics per susceptibility testing, anti-helminthic therapy, and intensive care, with improvement after about 12 days. The article notes common reservoirs for pathogenic E. coli: undercooked beef or poultry, raw leafy greens, unpasteurized dairy, and contaminated water from wells or rivers, plus contaminated surfaces. Symptoms range from diarrhea and abdominal pain to dehydration; severe cases risk hemolytic-uremic syndrome and sepsis.

article.articleHeadline: Discussing solutions to prevent disease outbreaks in livestock.
article.articleSummary: Quang Ngai Province, Vietnam, is intensifying anti-disease measures as African swine fever (ASF) spreads among livestock. Since the start of 2026, ASF-affected households reached 243 in 86 hamlets across 34 communes/wards, with 1,611 pigs infected, dead, or culled, and over 96.6 tons disposed. From early July to Aug 4, outbreaks expanded to 178 households in 19 communes, triggering the culling of 1,076 pigs and disposal of more than 59.2 tons. Outbreaks mainly involve smallholders with weak biosecurity. A highly virulent recombinant ASFV genotype I/II (rASFV I/II) complicates control and may reduce vaccine effectiveness. Other diseases include bovine lumpy skin disease (55 cases in 48 households across 19 communes; 36 cattle culled) and rabies (10 dogs culled; outbreak in Kon Tum ward not yet ended). Authorities distributed hundreds of thousands of vaccine doses, 13,500 liters of disinfectants, and conducted training/sampling across 96 communes.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue fever outbreak in Phu Quy Special Administrative-Economic Zone, many severe cases raise concerns.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever outbreak in Phu Quy Special Administrative-Economic Zone, Lam Dong Province, reports 82 cases and 6 severe cases as of August 4, 2026, the largest in years. All six hamlets on the island are affected. Phu An is the hotspot with 43 cases (over half) including two severe. Quy Thanh and My Khe each have 12 cases (two severe in Quy Thanh, one in My Khe). Triều Duong has 2 cases (one severe); Quy Hai and Phu Hai have fewer. Nine transmission foci identified; Phu An accounts for four, Quy Thanh three, My Khe one, Triều Duong one. Health authorities have addressed 7 of 9 foci, ending 6; 3 foci remain monitored, with one having a second chemical spray and two more spraying campaigns planned. Measures include mass environmental cleaning, larviciding, and fogging; nearly 2,000 households have been sprayed island-wide, with Phu An receiving two rounds. Residents are urged to eliminate breeding sites and seek early medical care upon fever to prevent severe dengue.

article.articleHeadline: Japanese Encephalitis: Why, even after vaccination, is it still necessary to verify that you have completed the full course of doses?
article.articleSummary: Japanese Encephalitis vaccination verification in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam: Parents may recall vaccination but not the number of doses, timing of the last dose, or whether a booster is due. Does 'vaccinated' mean 'fully vaccinated'? The program addressing this—titled “Japanese Encephalitis: Vaccination Right Not Enough, Fully Vaccinated Is Required”—features TTƯT.BS Trương Hữu Khanh, Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Infectious Diseases Association, and ThS.BS Nguyễn Hiền Minh, Deputy Head of the Immunization Unit at University of Medicine and Pharmacy Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City. They will explain how to review vaccination histories for late schedules, lost records, or vaccines given at multiple sites, and how to determine if a child is adequately protected. Airs at 19:00 on Thursday, 6 August 2026 in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

article.articleHeadline: Exposing the schemes to conceal nearly 1 metric ton of pork suspected of being infected with African swine fever.
article.articleSummary: In Hung Yen Province, Vietnam, authorities on 27 July uncovered a slaughter/processing facility run by Nguyen Trong Khoang? (Nguyễn Trọng Khương, born 1994) in Mỹ Hào Ward, Lỗ Xá, that handled pigs from multiple sources with non-fixed receiving points, processing off-site before storage in a home cold room. Khương allegedly disabled surveillance cameras and concealed the area to evade detection. A total of 977.8 kg of live animals and products were seized, with equipment used for slaughter and processing. Laboratory tests confirmed African swine fever virus in 7 of 9 samples. By 29 July the case was referred to the Hung Yen Provincial Police for prosecution under Article 317 (food safety violations). By 4 August, all animals and products tested positive for ASF and were destroyed in line with veterinary, food safety, and environmental protections. As of 6 August 2026, authorities continue action against the scheme.

article.articleHeadline: Guidelines for preventing gastrointestinal diseases and poisoning from drinking water sources.
article.articleSummary: Unsafe drinking water in Vietnam elevates the risk of acute gastrointestinal diseases—diarrhea, dysentery, typhoid—and food poisoning from microbial contamination (E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae), with possible viral and parasitic infections. Long-term exposure to heavy metals (arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium) and pesticides can accumulate, causing liver and kidney damage, neurodevelopment issues in children, and increased cancer risk. The Ministry of Health’s QCVN 01-1:2024/BYT sets 85 technical indicators across five groups for domestic water quality: microbiological (no E. coli or total coliform in 100 mL); physico-chemical (pH 6.0–8.5, turbidity ≤ 2 NTU, residual chlorine ≥ 0.2 mg/L at point of use); inorganic chemicals (e.g., arsenic ≤ 0.01 mg/L, lead ≤ 0.01 mg/L, nitrate ≤ 50 mg/L); organic pesticides (17 indicators); and radiological (α ≤ 0.1 Bq/L, β ≤ 1.0 Bq/L). Preventive measures include boiling, sealed storage, certified filtration (RO, Nano, UF) meeting QCVN for drinking water, regular tank cleaning (3–6 months), annual testing at provincial CDC labs, and protecting water sources.

article.articleHeadline: Prevent Zoonoses, Unisa Yogyakarta Supports Ban on the Trade of Rabies-Transmitting Animals
article.articleSummary: Unisa Yogyakarta backs the DIY Regional Council’s ban on trading rabies-transmitting animals—dogs, cats, civets, monkeys, and bats—to curb zoonotic risk in the Yogyakarta Special Region. Its UPT Integrated Laboratory, with a Halal Center, now applies high-accuracy DNA testing to verify halal status and detect pig DNA in meat, enabling BPOM and MUI to require lab-backed results for halal certification. The lab can sample street foods such as bakso to test for pig or other non-halal DNA, strengthening food safety oversight. Academics urge stronger enforcement via police and local government, including raids and sanctions on urban processing sites and forest-fringe areas. The university also operates Animal House for ethically approved animal experiments, sourcing pathogen-free mice, rats, and rabbits, supporting molecular research (ELISA, DNA) for drug development and downstream translational research.

article.articleHeadline: Amnesty Calls for MBG Suspension After Hundreds Fall Sick
article.articleSummary: Amnesty International Indonesia calls for suspension and a full review of the Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) program after suspected mass food poisoning linked to MBG meals sickened hundreds of students and teachers. As of August 5–6, 2026, incidents are reported in Jayapura, Papua, and Semarang, Central Java, with Depapre District (Jayapura Regency) reporting around 150 suspected cases after MBG meals on August 4, 2026. A July 28, 2026 incident affected at least 120 at a Jayapura public senior high school, and a July 31, 2026 incident at a Semarang public vocational high school affected about 707. Since MBG’s January 2025 launch, more than 37,000 students have reportedly been affected, including around 9,000 cases from January–May 2026. Symptoms include nausea, dizziness, weakness, vomiting, and diarrhea. Calls include supply-chain investigations, governance review, and accountability, amid constitutional and Komnas HAM rights concerns.

article.articleHeadline: Health professionals: The public should beware influenza and increased coughing during the dry season.
article.articleSummary: Jakarta health professionals report a rise in cough, fever, and runny nose during the dry season, caused by circulating influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 (lower activity). Symptoms: fever, cough, runny nose, sore throat, muscle aches, fatigue. Dr. Suci Nurika Haviza cites seasonal changes and close contact in schools and offices as drivers; poor rest, stress, and inadequate nutrition raise infection risk. High-risk groups: infants, toddlers, elderly, pregnant women, and people with chronic conditions such as asthma, diabetes, heart disease, and COPD. Prevention emphasizes handwashing, masks when sick, adequate rest, nutrition, and hydration; children should follow vaccination schedules, and adults at risk may consider influenza vaccination. Global week 29, 2026 shows seasonal patterns with influenza positivity below 10% and low SARS-CoV-2 activity; southern hemisphere reports around 15% influenza positivity in some areas; RSV remains low. WHO calls for strengthened surveillance for influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2.

article.articleHeadline: Monkey Causes Chaos in Indragiri Hilir Regency, Riau; 18 Residents Become Victims.

After a broad response by the Inhil Fire and Rescue Department (DPKP) and wildlife authorities, the macaque believed to be responsible was captured in a fruit-bait trap and then transported to Pekanbaru for identification by BBKSDA Riau to confirm its role. Authorities including police, the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI), BBKSDA, and community members helped manage the incident. Residents are urged to remain vigilant as the investigation continues; no fatalities were reported in this article.

article.articleHeadline: 482 Birds Without Quarantine Documents Prevented from Entering Bali, Posing a Risk of Spreading Disease.
article.articleSummary: On August 5, 2026, Balai Besar Karantina Hewan, Ikan, dan Tumbuhan Bali and partners intercepted 482 live birds transported by bus at Padangbai Port in Karangasem, Bali, without quarantine or health certificates. The birds, believed to originate from West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), included 258 pleci (Zosterops sp.), 95 Lonchura punctulata (glatik wingko), 85 Aplonis panayensis (cucak kombo), 16 Prinia familiaris (ciblek), 10 Pachycephala pectoralis (kancilan mas), 9 Pycnonotus zeylanicus (opyor jambul), 7 Cinnyris jugularis (madu sriganti), and 2 Lanius schach (cendet). None possessed animal health certificates. Authorities warned such shipments risk introducing animal diseases, notably avian influenza, threatening Bali's disease-free status and public health. The birds are quarantined for health screening; if cleared, they will be transferred to BKSDA for release into appropriate habitats, under joint oversight with TNI AL, KP3 Padangbai, and BKSDA Karangasem.

article.articleHeadline: Salmonella detected in pork from a Primorsky producer.
article.articleSummary: Salmonella detected in pork ham from a Primorsky Krai producer, Russia. Primorsky branch of the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) found Salmonella in a ready-to-cook pork semi-finished product after a 1.3 kg sample taken during production control at the plant; the July 27 protocol confirmed microbiological non-compliance. Salmonella survives freezing and can proliferate during thawing, but is fully destroyed by proper thermal processing; its presence in finished product indicates manufacturing regime violations. Since the start of 2026, the laboratory has documented Salmonella in meat semi-finished products in 10 cases. Earlier, Salmonella was detected in a meat semi-finished product from a producer in Ussuriysk district, Primorsky Territory. The pathogen was also found in 27 tons of frozen chicken hearts imported into Primorsky Krai from China, underscoring ongoing import/export-related risks.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies exposure is categorized into three levels, with different management approaches! A woman had her toes licked by a dog; the doctor deemed it a Category III exposure.
article.articleSummary: In Hangzhou, China, a park encounter ended with a stray dog licking a woman's toes. She sought care at Zhejiang Provincial People’s Hospital; examination revealed damaged skin around a toenail (paronychia). Clinicians classified the licking on broken skin as Category III rabies exposure, requiring both rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin (RIG). The article outlines a three-tier exposure system, with Category III covering puncture wounds or scratches, licking of broken skin, or mucous membrane contamination—warranting wound care, passive immunization, and active vaccination. A practical assessment tip is to wipe the contact area with alcohol; pain indicates possible skin disruption. It cautions that even in the absence of a bite, any licking of broken skin or mucous membranes by cats or dogs should prompt prompt medical evaluation. The report emphasizes the importance of timely post-exposure rabies management.

article.articleHeadline: A man who casually swatted a flying insect is forced to have his eyeball removed; the tiny biting midge has become a 'mobile source of infection'.
article.articleSummary: A Shenzhen man swatted a tiny moth fly (drain fly) from his left eyelid, rubbed the eye, and developed seasonal conjunctivitis with vision down to 0.02, later confirmed to involve Pseudomonas aeruginosa and culminating in enucleation of the left eyeball. In another case, an eight-year-old girl suffered over a month of vomiting live moth-fly larvae, diagnosed as drain fly larval intestinal infection; exposure likely from toilet and sink splashes spreading larvae to toothbrushes and cups, leading to ingestion. Conventional oral antiparasitics failed; resolution required thorough plumbing cleaning and elimination of the moth fly source. The common white-spotted moth fly (3–4 mm) carries bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa on its body; it breeds in pipes and drains, contaminating food, toiletries, and surfaces, and can cause ocular, oral, skin, and digestive infections, particularly in elderly, children, and immunocompromised individuals.

article.articleHeadline: Ganzhou CDC warmly reminds: In August, take precautions to prevent dengue fever, chikungunya fever, and other mosquito-borne infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: August in Ganzhou, Jiangxi, brings heat, humidity, and rainfall, boosting mosquito activity. The Ganzhou CDC warns of dengue fever and chikungunya fever, both spread by Aedes mosquitoes, with fever and rash. Respiratory illnesses—influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infection—are elevated, especially among the elderly and the chronically ill; symptoms include fever, cough, and sore throat. Travellers returning from Southeast Asia should perform 14-day self-monitoring and inform clinicians of travel history. Prevention: masks in crowded indoor spaces, handwashing, ventilation, and early medical care for symptoms. Enteric diseases rise with heat; mushroom poisoning is noted. Ensure safe drinking water, wash produce, fully cook meat/eggs/seafood, keep raw and cooked foods separate, and maintain kitchen hygiene. Seek care for diarrhea or jaundice. Rabies risk increases with dog/cat bites; vaccinate pets, leash animals, avoid stray wildlife. If exposed, wash wounds with soap and water for 15 minutes, disinfect, and seek vaccination within 24 hours, with immunoglobulin as indicated.

article.articleHeadline: Man in critical condition with multi-organ failure after outdoor fishing; scrub typhus nearly claimed his life.
article.articleSummary: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) caused a life-threatening illness in a 56-year-old man (Mr. Huang) in Wuhan, China, after outdoor fishing and field work. He developed dizziness, periorbital discomfort, and a fever up to 40°C, progressing to extensive bilateral pneumonia, septic shock, and multi-organ failure. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals, his condition worsened, requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressors. At Tongji Hospital (Huazhong University of Science and Technology), laboratory tests showed hypotension, thrombocytopenia, hepatic injury, pleural effusion, and cardiac dysfunction. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid gene testing confirmed Orientia tsutsugamushi infection, i.e., scrub typhus, a pathogen that often mimics influenza or cold in early stages and is notoriously difficult to diagnose promptly. The case highlights the need to consider scrub typhus in febrile patients with pneumonia and shock after outdoor exposure and to initiate targeted therapy promptly to avert organ failure.

article.articleSummary: On Aug 6, 2026, Sichuan-made, lyophilized human rabies vaccine (Vero cell) from Chengdu-based Sinovac Biotech received NMPA drug registration and market approval. The vaccine supports two regimens: a five-dose schedule (0, 3, 7, 14, 28 days) and a simplified four-dose schedule (0, 3, 7, 14 days), completing vaccination in as fast as 14 days. It is produced with a serum-free, animal-origin-free process, using ATCC-validated Vero cells (Vero-SF-ACF) and the rPV-2061 strain, via fixed-bed bioreactor perfusion, and is formulated as a 'five-zero' product (no serum, no animal materials, no preservatives, no antibiotics, no gelatin, no dextran). Phase III, randomized, double-blind data show 100% seroconversion by day 14 after first dose and at 3 months; at 6 months, seroconversion >97.5% (vs 96.47% for comparator). Adverse events were similar to comparator, with no vaccine-related serious events. Sichuan promotes vaccine clusters, including Tianfu Vaccine Valley in Chengdu.

article.articleHeadline: A scab on a wound doesn't mean it's healed; a woman scratched by her own cat was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis more than ten days later, nearly leading to amputation
article.articleSummary: Necrotizing fasciitis following a cat scratch in Xi’an, Shaanxi Province, China. A woman (pseudonym Zhao) sustained deep scratches on the foot and ankle from her pet cat. After initial wound cleaning, suturing, routine dressing, and rabies vaccination, she did not pursue follow-up; about ten days later she developed rapid swelling, warmth, and severe pain, diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis of the left lower leg and left Achilles tendon injury. Necrotizing fasciitis can rapidly erode deep fascia and soft tissue, risking sepsis and limb loss if treatment is delayed. To save the limb, the plastic surgery and burn reconstruction team performed staged surgeries under general anesthesia: first debridement with drainage and negative-pressure wound therapy, followed by a second-stage Achilles tendon repair, plus antibiotics and wound irrigation. After nearly a month, infection was controlled and discharge occurred; she is in rehabilitation. Clinicians urge timely management of animal bite/scratch wounds and strict follow-up to prevent fatal outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: Don't wade through standing water after rain; standing water harbors pathogens and can cause various diseases, warns the National CDC.
article.articleSummary: Following persistent rainfall, urban waterlogging has become severe in some Chinese cities. People are wading through floodwater for convenience. The National CDC warns that floodwater in cities can damage sewer and wastewater systems and mix with bacteria, viruses, and parasites, creating a reservoir of pathogens in standing water combined with sewage, silt, and garbage. Skin contact or exposure through broken skin to polluted floodwater can trigger skin infections, dermatitis, and gastrointestinal (enteric) infections. Stagnant water also fosters mosquitoes, increasing the risk of vector-borne diseases. During rain, avoid wading through water; if you must, minimize skin exposure and time spent in water. After returning home, thoroughly rinse and wash skin that has been in floodwater and keep skin clean and dry.

The regions reporting the highest case load were Cagayan Valley (458), the National Capital Region (412), Davao Region (265), and Caraga (263). Despite the drop, authorities urge continued vigilance during the rainy season. Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caused by Leptospira found in the urine of infected animals, especially rats, contaminating floodwater or mud. Infections can occur through broken skin or via eyes, nose, or mouth. Those who waded through floodwater should consult a doctor for appropriate treatment.

Cayenne Island reports three new active foci (now 10), and the sector remains in an epidemic-foci phase but stable. Since January, 244 hospitalizations for chikungunya at CHU de Guyane; 81% classic, 11% unusual, 7% severe; two deaths not directly linked to chikungunya. Dengue remains low with 11 cases. article.articleHeadline: Fewer mosquito bites, fewer transmissions: the scientific revolution against dengue is already underway - HSB News
article.articleSummary: Dengue control is increasingly driven by biotechnological strategies targeting the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The approach uses controlled releases of modified males to render offspring inviable or block virus transmission, notably via Wolbachia infection or the sterile insect technique (SIT), with some programs combining IIT-SIT. In Indonesia, Wolbachia releases reduced dengue cases by about 77% in treated areas. Singapore trials showed reductions in vector populations and transmission risk, and several field studies report >50% declines in dengue incidence with sustained efforts. Large-scale implementations include Brazil’s biofactory producing millions of mosquitoes weekly for release in high-risk zones, and Latin American programs that have protected millions and achieved ongoing case reductions. Advantages include avoidance of chemical pesticides, environmental sustainability, and reduced insecticide resistance, since males do not bite. Challenges include high upfront costs, community acceptance, local climate and density effects, and the need for long-term evidence; these strategies should complement traditional control.

Brazil, noting no PPA cases since 1984 thanks to border controls, herd monitoring, and private-sector biosecurity, hosts the Grupo de Prevención PPA Américas to coordinate regional prevention efforts among 21 member countries. Juan Luis Uccelli, coordinator, argues that PPA has no vaccine and can be latent, a 'time bomb,' and true eradication would require total culling of swine, as in the 1980s. While the continent aims for a PPA-free Dominican Republic, the missed opportunity in 2022 has raised pork costs.

article.articleSummary: Iracemápolis Municipal Health Department, São Paulo state, alerts the public to Brazilian spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) transmitted by Amblyomma ticks (star tick), as Brazil experiences a notable rise in cases this season. The disease can be severe and fatal if untreated. Incubation is 2–14 days after a tick bite; early signs include high fever, severe headache, muscle pains, chills, and malaise, followed by a red skin patch that does not blanch with pressure. Immediate healthcare should be sought for evaluation and diagnosis. Prevention emphasizes avoiding vegetation-rich areas, wearing long sleeves and pants, light-colored clothing, using insect repellents, and regularly inspecting and removing ticks. Domestic animals should receive veterinary treatment to control ticks. Health Secretary Ralf Silva stresses early detection for successful treatment. Exposed individuals should visit Family Health Units (USFs) or urgent care if fever and symptoms arise after forest or rural exposure. For more information, contact local health units.

article.articleHeadline: Live on Globo, Ana Maria Braga can't hide her reaction to learning of a measles outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Measles outbreak triggers targeted vaccination in São Paulo, Guarulhos, and São Bernardo do Campo, Brazil. During a live segment on Globo’s Mais Você, reporter Fabricio Battaglini explained that vaccination is directed at people up to 59 years old, leaving those over 60 not prioritized due to assumed prior exposure and natural immunity. Presenters, including 77-year-old Ana Maria Braga, questioned the rationale, asking what happens to individuals who never contracted measles and lack protection. Health authorities emphasized that the current goal is to contain localized outbreaks, with vaccination blocks activated in the affected municipalities to prevent spread. Brazil remains free of endemic measles circulation, but immunization is restricted to the age group advised by experts in the affected regions under the alert. The program provides a detailed campaign table summarizing discussion points.

article.articleHeadline: A deadly fungus that can infect cats and people is spreading
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-06, Sporothrix brasiliensis is driving a ginormous outbreak in Brazil, with spillover to cats, dogs and people in Paraguay, Chile, Argentina and Uruguay. Experts warn the fungus could reach the United States, potentially via a traveler bringing an infected cat. The pathogen lives as hyphae in soil but becomes contagious yeast in the body; transmission occurs through cat scratches or bites that inject the yeast, and through grooming that spreads it between cats. Sneezing can disseminate the yeast via air and contaminated surfaces, turning ordinary contact into a broader exposure risk. Dense cat populations—both urban and rural—facilitate spread, prompting calls for coordinated action by veterinarians, infection prevention, and public health to prevent introduction in the U.S. while noting concerns about spread in other large cities like Istanbul and Bangkok and in rural farm-cat settings.

article.articleHeadline: Guaratinguetá will conduct Yellow Fever vaccination campaign in the Rocinha region - Guaratinguetá Tourism Town City Hall.
article.articleSummary: Guaratinguetá’s City Hall, via the Municipal Health Secretariat, will conduct a Yellow Fever vaccination campaign on Saturday, August 8, 2026, from 08:00 to 15:00 in the Rocinha region. The event is door-to-door, bringing vaccination to residents and expanding access in rural areas. Neighbourhoods to be served include Paiol, Brumado, Fogueteiro de Cima, Pedra Branca, Goiabal, Fazendinha, Mandú, Retiro, Pinheirinho, Rincão, and Rodovia. Health teams will advise the public to keep their vaccination records up to date. The Yellow Fever vaccine is the primary preventive measure against a serious, potentially fatal disease. The initiative emphasizes care and prevention, especially given recent cases reported in municipalities within the region.

article.articleHeadline: Explosive diarrhea: an infection that has already killed two in the U.S. could reach Brazil?
article.articleSummary: Cyclospora-caused cyclosporiasis is driving a U.S. outbreak with 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases and about 11,500 suspected cases as of July 28, 2026, concentrated in Michigan where two deaths have been confirmed. The illness, nicknamed “explosive diarrhea,” stems from contaminated food or water rather than person-to-person spread; most infections respond to antibiotic treatment, though symptoms include profuse diarrhea, gas, nausea, and abdominal distension, with onset 7–10 days after exposure. The strongest suspicion points to lettuce from Taylor Farms grown in central Mexico, a supplier to Taco Bell, suggesting a foodborne origin. Brazilian risk appears low; authorities note such produce is not imported for Brazil’s consumption, and outbreaks in the Americas are not uncommon, with a 2000 outbreak in General Salgado, São Paulo, linked to the parasite (over 350 cases), plus later reports in Goiás. Immunosuppressed individuals face higher risk of severe disease.

article.articleHeadline: Invasive Mosquito Pushes Malaria Into Africa's Cities
article.articleSummary: Anopheles stephensi, an Asian malaria vector, is invading Africa’s cities, shifting malaria risk from rural to cities. Detected in Djibouti City in 2012, it has spread through the Horn of Africa and is tracked as far west as Ghana, with Ghana confirmed in 2024. A July 2026 Parasites & Vectors study confirmed urban transmission in Djibouti, finding 2 of 196 An. stephensi carrying Plasmodium vivax sporozoites; the haplotypes match Horn lineages. Unlike native vectors, An. stephensi breeds in water tanks, wells and construction sites, rests indoors and outdoors, bites by day, and feeds on livestock as well as people, undermining bed nets and indoor spraying. Ethiopian data show the species dominating districts (about 51% of sampled Anopheles). Kenya’s KEMRI and National Malaria Control Programme conduct national surveillance via Community Health Promoters. WHO vector alert; detection often lags. Westward spread toward megacities like Accra and Lagos is a key concern.

article.articleHeadline: An invasive malaria-carrying mosquito is spreading in Africa from India.
article.articleSummary: An invasive malaria-carrying mosquito, Anopheles stephensi, from India, is spreading rapidly across Africa, fueling malaria outbreak concerns in major urban centers. As of 2026-08-06, the World Health Organization warns that 126–130 million additional people may be at risk, especially in fast-growing African cities where malaria has been less common. An. stephensi thrives in densely populated urban areas, breeding in water containers around buildings, complicating control. It shows resistance to nearly all major insecticides. First detected in East Africa’s Djibouti in 2012, it has since reached Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana; Nigerian samples in 2024 indicate spread to West Africa. Researchers are pursuing biological control, innovative technologies, and next-generation insecticides. Monitoring is hampered by funding gaps and conflict, limiting knowledge of full distribution (Kenya Medical Research Institute).

article.articleHeadline: FAO Strengthens Brucellosis Diagnosis to Protect Livestock, Wildlife and Communities in KAZA
article.articleSummary: FAO strengthens brucellosis diagnosis in the Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA) with a five-day Complement Fixation Test (CFT) training at the Victoria Falls Wildlife Trust Veterinary Laboratory (20–24 July 2026), funded by EU STOSAR II and the Pandemic Fund. The program advances diagnostic capacity beyond initial Rose Bengal Plate Test screening toward confirmatory CFT testing at the wildlife–livestock interface, enabling timely detection in KAZA. Participants included veterinarians and laboratory technologists from the Victoria Falls Wildlife Trust, ZimParks, Zimbabwe’s Central Veterinary Laboratory, Bulawayo and Masvingo Provincial Labs, FAO Zambia and FAO Zimbabwe, with support from the KAZA Secretariat. The initiative reinforces One Health collaboration to reduce human health risks, protect communities, and bolster safer livestock production. Knowledge gains rose from 69% to 82% post-training, while Zimbabwe’s Central Veterinary Laboratory will continue mentorship and quality assurance across KAZA.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for a stronger response and international solidarity, according to Africa CDC.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Bundibugyo strain) worsens; since the outbreak was declared on May 15, 2026, the DRC has 3,973 confirmed cases and 1,801 deaths (case fatality >45%), with about 776 recoveries. The 17th outbreak has expanded from 9 to 51 health zones affected. Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya called for stronger international support to close critical response gaps and for studies on possible viral mutation. Major obstacles include limited contact-tracing capacity, rising community transmission, insufficient hospital beds, funding shortages, insecurity, and unsafe burials. Uganda is praised for interrupting local transmission, while 11 other African countries are deemed high-risk: South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia, Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Republic of the Congo, Burundi and Somalia.

article.articleHeadline: Brain-Eating Worm (Angiostrongylus cantonensis): Thai Man's Binge on Raw, Brined Seafood Causes Severe Intestinal Ulceration, Recurrent Massive Bleeding and Shock, Nearly Died
article.articleSummary: One Shanghai man, Xu (pseudonym), contracted Entamoeba histolytica after extensive consumption of raw and brined seafood during a business trip to Thailand. Upon return, he developed fulminant amebic enteritis with widespread intestinal ulcers, recurrent massive bleeding, and septic shock. Despite multiple surgeries, he remained critically ill, with severe inflammation, coagulation dysfunction, and hemoglobin dropping below 6 g/dL, risking intestinal perforation and death. He was transferred to Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center for emergency care, where a personalized, multidisciplinary treatment plan over more than 30 days controlled bleeding and infection, ultimately achieving survival. Entamoeba histolytica infections are common in tropical/subtropical regions; foodborne exposure through raw seafood is a notable risk. Travelers are advised to enforce strict food and water hygiene and seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, or vomiting, especially in hot weather. The report also notes parasitic risks associated with seafood consumption.
